lines.text: A land of forests, ice and two languages, built by fur traders, railways and quiet determination. This is the story of Canada, from Norse turf houses to today.
About the year 1000, Norse sailors built turf houses on the northern tip of Newfoundland. It is the only Norse settlement ever confirmed in North America.
Five centuries later Jacques Cartier sailed up the St Lawrence and claimed the land for France. He wrote down an Iroquoian word, kanata, and the country got its name.
New France grew along the great river and down to Louisiana, living on the fur trade and on alliances with many Native peoples.
The Englishman Henry Hudson searched the north for a route to Asia. His crew set him adrift in 1611, but his name stayed on the great bay.
Samuel de Champlain mapped the St Lawrence and the Great Lakes, and is remembered as the father of New France.
In 1608 he founded a trading post on the river that grew into Quebec City, still the only walled city north of Mexico.
In 1670 the Hudson's Bay Company was chartered to trade furs, and for two centuries it governed a vast territory around the bay.
In 1759, outside Quebec, the British under Wolfe defeated Montcalm's French. Both generals died, and New France passed to Britain.
When the Americans invaded in the War of 1812, the colonies held. No borders changed, but a Canadian feeling had begun to grow.
John A. Macdonald, born in Scotland, led the talks that joined the colonies, and in 1867 became Canada's first prime minister.
There is a darker thread too. For more than a century and a half, church-run residential schools took Indigenous children away from their families.
Louis Riel led the Metis in two risings in the west. He founded Manitoba, and after the second rising he was hanged for treason.
In 1845 Sir John Franklin's two ships sailed into the Arctic to find the Northwest Passage, and vanished. Their wrecks were found only in recent years.
With Confederation, the old heart of New France became the province of Quebec, French in its language and its pride.
And so in 1867 Canada was born, a federation of British colonies that would win full independence step by step.
In 1885 the Metis and First Nations rose again in Saskatchewan. Troops rode west on the new railway and crushed it in weeks.
That same year the last spike was driven at Craigellachie. The Canadian Pacific Railway now ran from Montreal to the Pacific.
In the Rockies, a protected hot spring grew into Banff, Canada's first national park of glaciers, lakes and forests.
Frederick Banting, a young doctor in Toronto, would go on to discover insulin with Charles Best.
In 1896 gold was found in the Yukon, and tens of thousands struggled north over the mountain passes to the Klondike. Few struck it rich.
Lester Pearson, a diplomat, would win the Nobel Peace Prize for proposing the first United Nations peacekeepers, and later lead the country.
In April 1917 all four Canadian divisions attacked Vimy Ridge together for the first time, and took it. Many see it as the moment Canada became a nation.
That December, a ship full of explosives collided in Halifax harbour and blew up, devastating the north end of the city.
Pierre Trudeau, prime minister for most of the seventies, made English and French official languages and brought the constitution home.
In 1922 insulin was given to a patient in Toronto for the first time, and diabetes no longer had to be a death sentence.
Toronto-born Frank Gehry grew up to design buildings of twisting metal, from Bilbao's Guggenheim to the Disney Concert Hall.
In 1931 the Statute of Westminster gave Canada full power to make its own laws.
Terry Fox lost a leg to cancer, then ran a marathon a day across Canada to raise money for research, until the cancer came back.
Wayne Gretzky, the Great One, rewrote hockey's scoring records, and his number ninety-nine was retired across the whole league.
In 1965, after a long debate, the red and white Maple Leaf flag rose over Parliament Hill for the first time.
Mark Carney, who would lead the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, became prime minister in the spring of 2025.
For Canada's hundredth birthday, Montreal held Expo 67, a world's fair built partly on new islands in the St Lawrence.
Three years later, in the October Crisis, Quebec separatists kidnapped two officials and the army was sent in.
Pierre Trudeau's son Justin would be prime minister himself, for a decade from 2015.
In 1976 Toronto's CN Tower opened, more than five hundred and fifty metres of concrete, the tallest free-standing structure on land for over thirty years.
In 1982 Canadians gained a Charter of Rights and Freedoms, written into their constitution.
The same act brought the constitution fully under Canada's control. Britain's parliament no longer had a say.
In 1995 Quebec voted on becoming a sovereign country. The No side won by about one point.
In 1999 Nunavut was carved from the Northwest Territories, a vast northern homeland governed mostly by the Inuit.
In 2010 Vancouver and Whistler hosted the Winter Olympics, and Canada won the most gold medals, men's hockey among them.
And in 2026 Canada shared the first World Cup played across three countries, with the United States and Mexico.
From a Norse camp to a shared World Cup, Canada keeps writing its story coast to coast.
